The systematic review on indoor cold for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines evaluates the health effects of indoor cold temperatures. The review aims to provide evidence to support the development of WHO guidelines. It builds on a 2014 review by Public Health England (PHE) and includes additional studies published after February 2014. The review examines the relationship between indoor temperatures below 18°C and health outcomes, focusing on vulnerable populations such as infants, young children, and older adults. The review identifies that colder indoor temperatures are associated with increased respiratory morbidity and mortality. For example, studies show that adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) experience better health outcomes when indoor temperatures are maintained at or above 21°C. Similarly, children with asthma show improved lung function with higher indoor temperatures. However, some studies, such as those on upper respiratory tract infections in children, show no consistent association with indoor temperature. Regarding cardiovascular health, lower indoor temperatures are linked to higher blood pressure. Studies from Japan and Scotland demonstrate that individuals living in colder homes have a greater risk of elevated blood pressure. Laboratory studies also suggest that warming reduces blood pressure, but these findings are considered indirect evidence. The certainty of evidence that warming cold homes to a minimum of 18°C reduces cardiovascular morbidity and mortality is assessed as moderate. The review concludes that maintaining indoor temperatures of at least 18°C in winter minimizes health risks, particularly for vulnerable populations. It emphasizes the importance of considering the context in which evidence is collected, as indoor and outdoor temperature exposures differ significantly. The findings support the development of housing and health guidelines to improve thermal environments and reduce health risks associated with indoor cold.
